Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: Conjugating the diagonal sum in [F5] entry by entry and using [F2] gives $\overline{\operatorname{tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{tr}((AB)^*)$. For $n=0$, both sides are the empty sum $0$.
By [F1] and [F3], $(AB)^*=B^*A^*=BA$. Then [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}(BA)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$, so step 1.1 says $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ equals its conjugate and is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Let $R=P^{1/2}$ from [F2] and put $T=RQR$. Since $Q$ is nonnegative by [F1], self-adjointness of $R$ and the inner-product identity [F5] give $\langle Tx,x\rangle=\langle QRx,Rx\rangle\ge0$ for every $x$. Thus every diagonal entry $\langle Te_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal coordinate basis is nonnegative real; summing by [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}(T)\ge0$. This also holds in dimension zero because the trace is the empty sum.
Since $P=R^2$, [F3] applied to $U=R$ and $V=RQ$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)=\operatorname{tr}(R(RQ))=\operatorname{tr}((RQ)R)=\operatorname{tr}(RQR)=\operatorname{tr}(T)\ge0$ by step 1.1.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $I_H:H\to H$ denote the identity map $x\mapsto x$. An **effect** on $H$ is an endomorphism $E$ such that both $E$ and $I_H-E$ are non-negative in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. A **finite complete positive family** is a nonempty finite list $(E_1,\ldots,E_n)$ of non-negative endomorphisms with $\sum_{a=1}^n E_a=I_H$. The next lemma proves that every member of such a family is an effect, so the family is a finite complete effect family. This is algebraic data only; it does not assert a measurement law.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$
If $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are positive semidefinite, then $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)\ge0$ for every $n\ge0$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: Since $M=M^*$, $MM^*=M^2=M^*M$, so [F1] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $Me_k=\lambda_ke_k$. For each unit $e_k$, [F2] and [F3] give $\lambda_k=\langle Me_k,e_k\rangle=\langle e_k,Me_k\rangle=\overline{\lambda_k}$, so $\lambda_k$ is real; [F13] gives $|\lambda_k|=\|Me_k\|\le\|M\|\le1$. Thus the eigenvalues $(1\pm\lambda_k)/2$ of $E_\pm$ and those of $I-E_\pm$ are nonnegative, so both operators are nonnegative and each $E_\pm$ is an effect by [F4] and [F5]. Direct addition gives $E_++E_-=I$, hence the pair is a two-outcome POVM by [F6].

By [F6], the outcome weights are $p_\pm=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_\pm)$; representing endomorphisms in the orthonormal basis from step 1.1, [F9] makes them nonnegative. By [F8], [F11], [F7], and $E_++E_-=I$, their sum is $p_++p_-=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(E_++E_-))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$. Their signed mean is $p_+-p_-=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(E_+-E_-))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho M)=\operatorname{tr}(M\rho)$ by [F8] and [F12], and it is real by [F10]. Thus the outcome law has mean $\operatorname{tr}(M\rho)$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
normal, and write the spectral resolution from
[[thm-spectral-resolution-and-polynomial-spectral-projections]] as

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

where the $\lambda_j$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$ and $P_j$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$. For a function
$f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$ on the spectrum of $T$, define

$$f(T):=\sum_{j=1}^r f(\lambda_j)P_j.$$

This is the **spectral functional calculus** of $T$. For the identity function
$\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}$, one has $\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}(T)=T$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, let $T:V\to V$ be
normal, and write the spectral resolution from
[[thm-spectral-resolution-and-polynomial-spectral-projections]] as

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

where the $\lambda_j$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$ and $P_j$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$. For a function
$f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$ on the spectrum of $T$, define

$$f(T):=\sum_{j=1}^r f(\lambda_j)P_j.$$

This is the **spectral functional calculus** of $T$. For the identity function
$\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}$, one has $\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}(T)=T$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. **Signs.** If $a \ge 0$ then $a^n \ge 0$, and if $a > 0$ then $a^n > 0$.
2. **Strict monotonicity in the base.** If $0 \le a < b$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n < b^n$. Consequently, for $a, b \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$: $a < b \iff a^n < b^n$ and $a \le b \iff a^n \le b^n$, and $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with the base.** If $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; if $a > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a > 1$; and if $0 \le a \le 1$ then $a^n \le 1$.
4. **Monotonicity in the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^m < a^n$ whenever $m < n$ in $\mathbb{N}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^n = 1$ for all $n$; and if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^m > a^n$ whenever $m < n$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

$$\sup\{\operatorname{tr}(CX):X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n},\ X\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}(A_jX)\le b_j\ (1\le j\le m)\},$$
and its declared **dual program** is
$$\inf\{b\cdot y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ y_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^m y_jA_j-C\succeq0\}.$$
Here $X\succeq0$ and $D\succeq0$ mean positive semidefinite in the finite-dimensional quadratic-form sense. Primal and dual feasibility, boundedness, attainment, trace bounds, sparsity, and normalizations such as $A_1=I,b_1=R$ are separate promises and do not follow from this definition.

citations.quote: For $n\ge1$, a round count $T\ge1$, and Hermitian losses $M_1,\ldots,M_T\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $-I\preceq M_t\preceq I$, choose $0<\eta\le1$. Define $S_0=0$, $S_t=\sum_{s=1}^tM_s$, $W_t=e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}$, and $\rho_t=W_t/\operatorname{tr}(W_t)$. The round cost is $\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)$. The exponential is the finite-dimensional Hermitian spectral functional calculus. Loss matrices, access to them, and the classical or quantum work to construct them are input costs.

For $0<\eta\le1$ and $x\in[-1,1]$,
$$\exp(-\eta x)\le1-\eta x+\eta^2.$$
Consequently, if $M=M^*$ and $-I\preceq M\preceq I$, then $\exp(-\eta M)\preceq I-\eta M+\eta^2I$.

For Hermitian matrices $H,K\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$ with $p\ge1$,
$$\operatorname{tr}\exp(H+K)\le\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\exp(H)\exp(K)\bigr).$$
Here $\exp(A)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}A^j/j!$ is the norm-convergent finite-matrix exponential series. No commutativity assumption is imposed.
If $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ are positive semidefinite, then $\operatorname{tr}(PQ)\ge0$ for every $n\ge0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

derivations.claim: Put $Z_t=\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\eta S_t})$ and $m_t=\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)$. By [F5], write $M_t=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^*$; the loss bounds imply $\lambda_k\in[-1,1]$. The matrix $\sigma=U^*\rho_tU$ is positive with trace one by [F1] and [F7]. Thus $q_k=\sigma_{kk}\ge0$ and $\sum_kq_k=1$. Trace cyclicity and the diagonal-sum formula give $m_t=\sum_k\lambda_kq_k\in[-1,1]$, consistently with [F6]. Hence $1-\eta m_t+\eta^2\ge1-\eta+\eta^2=(\eta-1/2)^2+3/4>0$. Since $S_t$ is Hermitian, Golden–Thompson [F3] gives $Z_t\le\operatorname{tr}(e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}e^{-\eta M_t})$. By [F2], $(I-\eta M_t+\eta^2I)-e^{-\eta M_t}\succeq0$; [F4] compares its trace product with the positive matrix $e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}$, and [F9] expands the result as $Z_t\le Z_{t-1}(1-\eta m_t+\eta^2)$. Put $s=-\eta m_t+\eta^2$, so $s\ge\eta^2-\eta\ge-1/4$. If $s\ge0$, the series [F8] gives $\exp(s)\ge1+s$. If $s=-v$ with $0<v\le1/4$, absolute convergence [F8] permits pairing the tail after its linear term as $\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{v^{2j+2}}{(2j+2)!}(1-\frac{v}{2j+3})\ge0$, so again $\exp(s)\ge1+s$. Therefore $Z_t\le Z_{t-1}\exp(-\eta m_t+\eta^2)$.

Iterating step 1.1 from $Z_0=n$ gives $Z_T\le n\exp(-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T)$. If $S_T$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, [F5] gives $Z_T=\sum_ke^{-\eta\lambda_k}\ge\exp(-\eta\lambda_{\min}(S_T))$. Since $n>0$, [F10]–[F11] give $n\exp(-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T)=\exp(\ln n-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T)$. Strict increase of $\exp$ and the inverse relation in [F10] therefore imply $-\eta\lambda_{\min}(S_T)\le\ln n-\eta\sum_tm_t+\eta^2T$. Rearranging and dividing by $\eta>0$ proves the inequality.

Fix integers $n\ge0$ and $m\ge0$, Hermitian matrices $C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The **primal semidefinite program** is
$$\sup\{\operatorname{tr}(CX):X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n},\ X\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}(A_jX)\le b_j\ (1\le j\le m)\},$$
and its declared **dual program** is
$$\inf\{b\cdot y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ y_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^m y_jA_j-C\succeq0\}.$$
Here $X\succeq0$ and $D\succeq0$ mean positive semidefinite in the finite-dimensional quadratic-form sense. By [[lem-qa-30-hermitian-product-trace-real]], all displayed trace objectives and constraints are real. Primal and dual feasibility, boundedness, attainment, trace bounds, sparsity, and normalizations such as $A_1=I,b_1=R$ are separate promises and do not follow from this definition.

The sign convention is maximize for the primal, minimize for the dual, $\le$ for primal scalar constraints, nonnegative dual multipliers, and dual slack $\sum_jy_jA_j-C\succeq0$.

For $n\ge1$, a round count $T\ge1$, and Hermitian losses $M_1,\ldots,M_T\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $-I\preceq M_t\preceq I$, choose $0<\eta\le1$. Define $S_0=0$, $S_t=\sum_{s=1}^tM_s$, $W_t=e^{-\eta S_{t-1}}$, and $\rho_t=W_t/\operatorname{tr}(W_t)$. The round cost is $\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)$. The exponential is the finite-dimensional Hermitian spectral functional calculus. Loss matrices, access to them, and the classical or quantum work to construct them are input costs.

Let $n\ge1$, $T\ge1$, $0<\eta\le1$, and let $M_1,\ldots,M_T$ be Hermitian with $-I\preceq M_t\preceq I$. For the update of [[def-qa-30-mmw-game]],
$$\sum_{t=1}^T\operatorname{tr}(M_t\rho_t)\le\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^TM_t\right)+\eta T+\frac{\ln n}{\eta}.$$

derivations.claim: By $\|A_j\|,\|C\|\le1$ and $\|y_t\|_1\le r$, the triangle inequality gives $\|M_t\|\le(r+1)/w=1$, so the regret bound applies. Sum the lower bounds from step 1.1 and combine them with [F3]. Writing $S=\sum_tM_t$, we get $-2\theta T\le\lambda_{\min}(S)+\eta T+\ln(n)/\eta$, hence $\lambda_{\min}(S/T)\ge-(2\theta+\eta+\ln(n)/(\eta T))$.

The dual slack of $\bar y$ is $\sum_j\bar y_jA_j-C=\gamma I+(w/T)S$, because the identity coefficient contributes $\gamma A_1=\gamma I$. Step 2.1 and the lower bound on $\gamma$ make this matrix positive semidefinite. Also $\bar y\ge0$ and $b\cdot\bar y=\gamma R+T^{-1}\sum_tb\cdot y_t\le\gamma R+\alpha$. Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.
For Hermitian matrices $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge0$, the trace $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ is real.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

normal, and write the spectral resolution from
[[thm-spectral-resolution-and-polynomial-spectral-projections]] as

$$T=\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j P_j,$$

where the $\lambda_j$ are the distinct eigenvalues of $T$ and $P_j$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $E_{\lambda_j}(T)$. For a function
$f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C$ on the spectrum of $T$, define

$$f(T):=\sum_{j=1}^r f(\lambda_j)P_j.$$

This is the **spectral functional calculus** of $T$. For the identity function
$\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}$, one has $\operatorname{id}_{\sigma(T)}(T)=T$.

For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

derivations.claim: By [F3]–[F4], write the spectral projections of $P$ as $\Pi_+,\Pi_-$ (either may be zero), so $e^{-i\theta P/2}=\exp(-i\theta/2)\Pi_++\exp(i\theta/2)\Pi_-$. Euler's formula [F5] and parity [F6] give $e^{-i\theta P/2}=\cos(\theta/2)I-i\sin(\theta/2)P$. Absorb all other fixed circuit factors into fixed vectors/operators and expand the expectation bilinearly. Products of the two trigonometric factors reduce by [F7] to $C(\theta)=a+b\cos\theta+c\sin\theta$ for constants independent of $\theta$.

By [F8], differentiation gives $C'(\theta)=-b\sin\theta+c\cos\theta$. The shift formulas [F9] give $C(\theta+\pi/2)-C(\theta-\pi/2)=2(-b\sin\theta+c\cos\theta)$, proving the formula. For a finite sum of such expectation terms, differentiation and the shifted difference both distribute linearly.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph, $p\ge1$, and $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_p,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p\in\mathbb R$. On $|V|$ qubits define
$$C_G=\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\frac{I-Z_uZ_v}{2},\qquad B_G=\sum_{v\in V}X_v.$$
Prepare $|+\rangle^{\otimes |V|}$ and apply, in the declared right-to-left product convention,
$$U_{G,p}(\gamma,\beta)=\prod_{j=p}^{1}e^{-i\beta_jB_G}e^{-i\gamma_jC_G}.$$
The output state is $|\psi_{G,p}(\gamma,\beta)\rangle=U_{G,p}|+\rangle^{\otimes|V|}$ and the objective is $\langle\psi|C_G|\psi\rangle_D$. Measuring every qubit in the computational basis returns a random bitstring, hence a cut. Each cost and mixer exponential, graph-input access, parameter encoding, state preparation, measurement, repetition, and classical optimizer cost must be supplied and charged; this definition is not a guarantee of a maximum cut or approximation ratio.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

For a finite-dimensional unitary $U$, **inverse access** is the explicitly granted operation $U^\dagger=U^{-1}$. Its availability and query or gate charge are recorded separately from forward access, including any controlled access in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For a chronological sequence of length $k\ge0$ that applies $U_1$ first and $U_k$ last, the total operator is $W=U_k\cdots U_1$ when $k>0$ and $W=I_H$ when $k=0$. For $k>0$, the inverse sequence applies $U_k^\dagger$ first, then $U_{k-1}^\dagger$, down to $U_1^\dagger$; for $k=0$ it is the empty sequence.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Its **endomorphisms** are its complex-linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]); for an endomorphism $P$, $P^*$ denotes its adjoint, which exists uniquely in finite dimension ([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]], [[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]). A **finite projective measurement** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $(P_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ of endomorphisms such that

$$P_a^*=P_a,\qquad P_a^2=P_a,\qquad P_aP_b=0\ (a\ne b),\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}P_a=I_H.$$

The products above are compositions, the sum is pointwise addition of endomorphisms, and $I_H$ is the identity map; these operations preserve linear maps ([[prop-linear-maps-form-a-vector-space]], [[lem-composition-and-identity-linear-maps]]). The projections $P_a=0$ are permitted. For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (nonnegative and trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), the associated outcome weights are $p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_a)$; their nonnegativity and normalization are proved in [[thm-qc-projective-measurement-outcome-law]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

derivations.claim: If $p=1$, the direct flag outcome is good. If $0<p<1$, put $u=\sqrt{1-p}$, $v=\sqrt p$, $z=u+iv$, and $\xi=z^2=a+i\beta$, so $a=1-2p$ and $\beta=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}$. The orthonormal vectors $|B\rangle=(I-\Pi)|\psi\rangle/u$ and $|G\rangle=\Pi|\psi\rangle/v$ give $|\psi\rangle=u|B\rangle+v|G\rangle$. In this ordered basis the reflection about $|\psi\rangle$ is $\begin{pmatrix}a&\beta\\\beta&-a\end{pmatrix}$ and $I-2\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, so one Grover iteration has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&-\beta\\\beta&a\end{pmatrix}$. It multiplies the complex coordinate $u+iv$ by $\xi$, hence after $j$ iterations the good amplitude is $\operatorname{Im}(\xi^jz)=\operatorname{Im}(z^{2j+1})$.

If $p_{\rm low}<1/2$, then $K\ge2$ and minimality of $b=\lceil\log_2K\rceil$ gives $K/2^b\ge1/2$. Conditional on $J<K$, the draw is uniform on $0,\ldots,K-1$. For $p\le1/2$, $(\operatorname{Im}w)^2=(1-\operatorname{Re}(w^2))/2$ and the finite geometric sum of $\xi^{2j+1}$ give $$\frac1K\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Im}(z^{2j+1})\bigr)^2=\frac12-\frac{\operatorname{Im}(\xi^{2K})}{4K\beta}\ge\frac12-\frac1{4K\beta}.$$ Here $\beta=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\ge\sqrt{2p}$ and $K\ge1/\sqrt{p_{\rm low}}$, so $K\beta\ge\sqrt2$ and the conditional mean success exceeds $1/8$. Multiplication by $\Pr(J<K)\ge1/2$ gives randomized-branch success at least $1/16$. For $p>1/2$ the direct flag succeeds with probability greater than $1/2$.

If $p\le1/2$, the direct-then-randomized round succeeds with probability at least $1/16$ by step 2.1; if $p>1/2$ or $p_{\rm low}\ge1/2$, its direct flag succeeds with probability at least $1/2$. Independent fresh rounds therefore fail altogether with probability at most $(15/16)^N\le\rho$ by the exact cap test. The comparison loop terminates because $(16/15)^N=(1+1/15)^N\ge1+N/15$ by the binomial theorem, so $(15/16)^N\le15/(15+N)\to0$. If $N>1$, minimality gives $(15/16)^{N-1}>\rho$; applying the increasing logarithm and using $\ln((16/15)^{N-1})=(N-1)\ln(16/15)$, with $\ln(16/15)>0$, gives $N-1<\ln(1/\rho)/\ln(16/15)$. The same asymptotic bound holds for $N=1$, so $N=O(1+\ln(1/\rho))$. Since $K=O(p_{\rm low}^{-1/2})$, the stated call bound follows.

Every successful branch is passed through the supplied flag-only instrument, so its returned state is the normalized good projection of that branch's input and no score, label, or work register is measured. Step 1.1 shows that each amplified good component is a scalar multiple of $|G\rangle$; direct success has the same good ray. Thus every successful return is $\Pi V|0\rangle/\sqrt p$ up to global phase. Each round uses at most $K-1$ Grover iterations, one direct preparation, at most one amplified preparation, and $b$ random bits; multiplying by $N$ proves the stated call and random-bit bounds, with each controlled, inverse, reflection, verifier, and output cost charged.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

For an integer matrix dimension $d\ge1$, define the maximally entangled reference vector
$$|\Phi_d\rangle=d^{-1/2}\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}|i\rangle|i\rangle$$
on two ordered $d$-dimensional registers. The access contract supplies a finite preparation unitary $V_\Phi$, its inverse, width/ancillas, input encoding, and costs $C_\Phi$, satisfying $V_\Phi(|0\rangle|0\rangle|0^a\rangle)=|\Phi_d\rangle|0^a\rangle$ exactly in the declared encoding. Its action on other inputs is any supplied unitary completion; the inverse is that of the complete unitary. When $d=2^q$, a concrete preparation applies $H$ to each of the $q$ first-register qubits and then CNOT from each first-register qubit to its matching second-register qubit, using exactly $q$ Hadamards and $q$ CNOTs on $2q$ wires. For other $d$, $V_\Phi$ and its cost are supplied inputs satisfying the same preparation equation; unused encoded labels have zero output amplitude, and no padding is allowed unless its effect on traces is accounted for.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Let $n,m\ge0$ and let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ be a total Boolean function on ordered bit strings. Its coherent XOR oracle is the linear extension of
$$
O_f|x,y\rangle=|x,y\oplus f(x)\rangle
$$
on the ordered input and target computational basis, where XOR is componentwise. The declared access contract states how many invocations count as queries and whether a controlled invocation is supplied. A query to this declared black box is counted separately from elementary gate size, depth, and width.

If $f$ is supplied instead by an explicit Boolean circuit, implementing $O_f$ means compiling that circuit and paying its reversible elementary-gate and workspace costs; the function description alone is not a free query. For this XOR oracle, its inverse is the same map, as proved in [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Controlled access remains a separate capability unless the contract explicitly provides it.

For a finite-dimensional unitary $U$, **inverse access** is the explicitly granted operation $U^\dagger=U^{-1}$. Its availability and query or gate charge are recorded separately from forward access, including any controlled access in [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For a chronological sequence of length $k\ge0$ that applies $U_1$ first and $U_k$ last, the total operator is $W=U_k\cdots U_1$ when $k>0$ and $W=I_H$ when $k=0$. For $k>0$, the inverse sequence applies $U_k^\dagger$ first, then $U_{k-1}^\dagger$, down to $U_1^\dagger$; for $k=0$ it is the empty sequence.

Let $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$ be a closed convex body in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. In any rotated coordinates set $C=\{y:\exists t,(y,t)\in K\}$ and $h(y)=\min\{t:(y,t)\in K\}$. Then $h$ is convex, finite on $B(0,r)$, and $L=2R/r$-Lipschitz on $B(0,r/2)$. Every interior point of $C$ has a subgradient, and every such subgradient at a point in the interior of this ball has norm at most $L$.

For $\|y\|\le r/2$, a $\mathrm{MEM}_{\varepsilon,0}$ query at $(y,t)$, $t\le-r/2$, has these implications: an IN answer implies $t\ge h(y)-3R\varepsilon/r$; an OUT answer implies $t\le h(y)+2R\varepsilon/r$. Hence binary search on $[-R,-r/2]$, returning its final upper endpoint when its width is at most $\delta/3$, approximates $h(y)$ within $\delta$ if $\varepsilon\le r\delta/(3R)$. It uses $O(1+\log(R/\delta))$ membership queries and has a clean coherent implementation using the same order of queries and inverse queries.

Finally, let $a\ge0$. If $x=-\|x\|e_n$ receives OUT and $h(y)\ge h(0)+\langle v,y\rangle-a\|y\|-b$ on $C$, then $s=(-v,1)/\|(-v,1)\|$ satisfies $\langle s,z\rangle\ge\langle s,x\rangle-aR-b-2R\varepsilon/r$ for every $z\in K$.

Let $1\le d\le n$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. Let $r_1,L>0$ and suppose $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of $[-2r_1,2r_1]^d\subset C$, with every point there having a subgradient in $\mathbb R^d$ of norm at most $L$. Let $0<\rho\le1/3$, $\rho_0=99\rho/100$, $0<\delta\le nr_1L/\rho_0$, and $r_2=\sqrt{\delta r_1\rho_0/(nL)}$. A deterministic clean value oracle approximates $f$ to error at most $\delta$ on the finite query grids.

Choose a finite uniform grid of cell centers of $[-r_1,r_1]^d$, with $2^b$ cells per coordinate and mesh $h_0=2r_1/2^b\le(\rho/1000)r_2^2/(8n^2r_1)$. Sample one center $z$ uniformly using $b$ independent fair bits per coordinate, and keep it fixed across all subsequent runs. Put $a=2r_2/n$, $B=La$, $m=\max\{5,\lceil\log_2(B/(28\pi\delta))\rceil\}$, $M=2^m$, and $B_*=28\pi\delta M$. On each independent run prepare the uniform product grid $u_i=(j_i+1/2)/M-1/2$, apply phase $\exp(2\pi iM\widetilde f(z+au)/(3B_*))$ with clean uncomputation, apply the negative-sign QFT to each coordinate, and decode signed integers $y_i$ as $3B_*y_i/(aM)$. Use $N=\lceil18\ln(1000n/\rho)+3\rceil$ independent runs and coordinate medians. A total implemented-phase operator error at most $1/1000$ per run is permitted.

With probability at least $1-\rho$, the resulting vector $v\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfies, simultaneously for every $y\in C$,
$$f(y)\ge f(0)+\langle v,y\rangle-(23n)^2\sqrt{\frac{\delta L}{\rho_0r_1}}\|y\|-2L\sqrt n\,r_1.$$
The number of value-oracle and inverse calls is $O(\log(n/\rho))$. Random bits, phases, QFT gates, arithmetic, and output costs are separate.

Let $B(x,t)=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\|z-x\|_2\le t\}$ and let $B(K,t)=\bigcup_{x\in K}B(x,t)$ for $t\ge0$; $B(K,-t)$ denotes the inward erosion consisting of points whose radius-$t$ ball is contained in $K$. A convex body is a closed convex set with nonempty interior. Assume rationally encoded $0<r\le R$ and $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$. The deterministic weak-membership oracle $\mathrm{MEM}_{\varepsilon,0}(K)$ is queried at a finite-precision point $y$ and must correctly assert either $y\in B(K,\varepsilon)$ or $y\notin B(K,-\varepsilon)$. In the overlap it may return either valid assertion. The coherent interface is a supplied reversible Boolean unitary with a fixed deterministic completion on every encoded input, together with its inverse and any controlled forms used.

A weak separation oracle $\mathrm{SEP}_{\eta,\rho}(K)$, queried at $y$, with probability at least $1-\rho$, either asserts $y\in B(K,\eta)$ or asserts $y\notin B(K,-\eta)$ and returns a unit vector $g$ satisfying $\langle g,z\rangle\le\langle g,y\rangle+\eta$ for every $z\in B(K,-\eta)$. The membership-to-separation algorithm is promised only on the query domain in its theorem; no unique answer is required in the boundary bands. A finite unit-normal encoding may be a nonzero rational vector v with the normalization g=v/||v|| interpreted exactly; rational bisection supplies an upper norm bound N between ||v|| and2||v|| when a classical reduction requires rational halfspaces. Radius, point, unit-normal and offset encodings and all query/inverse/gate/bit costs are part of the contract.

This specifies oracle behavior; a membership-to-separation theorem and any separation-to-optimization composition are separate claims with their own hypotheses.

This finite algorithm takes a convex body, a rational query point and radii, a precision/failure budget, and supplied coherent deterministic weak-membership access with inverse. It returns IN when the membership interface certifies that branch; otherwise it returns a finite-precision weak separating normal and halfspace or an explicitly distinguished INVALID, RANDOM_FAIL, or FAILURE branch. The algorithm charges the membership oracle and inverse, all controlled queries, point rotations, numerical arithmetic, random sampling, phase estimation, QFTs, output bits, and every gate.

Assume countable choice, with positive rationally encoded radii and accuracy/failure parameters. Let $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$ be a closed convex body, let $0<\zeta\le R$, $0<\nu\le1/3$, and let $c$ be a unit objective vector with supplied finite rational approximations to any requested error. Put
$$\tau=\zeta/8,\qquad s=r\tau/(16R),\qquad \eta=s/(100n).$$
Let $T$ be the least integer with $(3/4)^T(2R)^n<(2s/n)^n$, and $B$ the least positive integer with $2^B\tau\ge8R$. There is a finite classical procedure using at most $BT=O(n\log(nR/s)(1+\log(R/\zeta)))$ calls to $\mathrm{SEP}_{\eta,\nu/(2BT)}(K)$ that, with probability at least $1-\nu$, returns $y\in B(K,\zeta)$ with
$$\langle c,y\rangle\ge\max_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle-\zeta.$$
The normal encoding must supply a nonzero rational direction $u$ for its unit normal $u/\|u\|$; a rational $N$ with $\|u\|\le N\le2\|u\|$ can be computed by bisection. Query points and polytope arithmetic are rational. Computing exact centroids by exhaustive finite triangulation is allowed and charged separately: this result asserts no polynomial arithmetic, gate, or bit-time bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If the supplied boundary width is smaller than half its positive admissible upper bound, regard the same oracle as having that larger width. Its two assertions remain valid because outer bands enlarge and inward erosions shrink; the same is true for an exact zero-width oracle. Write $\varepsilon>0$ for this working allowance, which still satisfies the displayed input bound. First query membership at $x$. IN implies $x\in B(K,\varepsilon)\subseteq B(K,\eta)$, which is a permitted output. OUT implies $x\notin B(K,-\varepsilon)$, hence $x\notin B(K,-\eta)$ since inward erosions decrease with their radius. For $n=1$, $K$ is an interval containing $[-r,r]$ and $\varepsilon<r/2$. A positive OUT point must be at or beyond the positive endpoint minus $\varepsilon$; a negative one has the analogous property. Its outward signed normal therefore satisfies the separation contract with slack at most $\varepsilon$. The point zero necessarily has an IN answer. This proves the scalar case with a single query.

Suppose $n\ge2$ and OUT occurs. Rotate $x$ to $-\|x\|e_n$ and use the height function of [F1]. Set $L=2R/r$, $\rho_0=99\rho/100$, $r_1=r\eta/(12\sqrt nR)$ and $$\delta=\frac{\eta\rho_0 n^{-9/2}}{96\cdot23^4}\left(\frac{r\eta}{R^2}\right)^2.$$ Then $[-2r_1,2r_1]^{n-1}\subseteq B(0,r/2)$ since $2\sqrt n r_1\le r/6$. Moreover $\delta\le nr_1L/\rho_0$, by substituting $r_1,L$, $r\le R$, $\eta\le R$ and $\rho_0\le1/3$. Thus the height and grid lemma hypotheses hold.

Substitution of the input bound shows $\varepsilon<0.97\,r\delta/(3R)$: squaring verifies $58^9>(300\cdot23^4)^2$, while the remaining factor is at most $288/(300\cdot0.99)<0.97$. The deterministic address perturbation in [F4] is at most $\varepsilon/1000$ and its height displacement at most $\delta/1000$. Thus effective membership uncertainty is less than $0.98\,r\delta/(3R)$. The lower height error is less than $0.98\delta$, and the upper one is at most $2(0.98)\delta/3+\delta/3<0.987\delta$ before the additional $\delta/1000$ value rounding. Hence the implemented clean height-value oracle has uniform error below $\delta$. Binary search and its inverse use $O(1+\log(R/\delta))$ membership/inverse calls by [F1]. This explicit slack also permits the certified rotation/address rounding in [F4]; those are bit costs, not uncounted queries.

Apply [F2] to the transverse dimension $d=n-1$, using its finite shift and $M\ge32$ grid. With failure probability at most $\rho$, it returns $g$ satisfying $$h(y)\ge h(0)+\langle g,y\rangle-(23n)^2\sqrt{\delta L/(\rho_0r_1)}\|y\|-2L\sqrt n r_1.$$ The parameter substitutions are exact: $2L\sqrt n r_1=\eta/3$ and $(23n)^2\sqrt{\delta L/(\rho_0r_1)}=\eta/(2R)$. No differentiability of $h$ or exact membership at boundary points is used.

The finite shift uses no membership query. There are $O(\log(n/\rho))$ phase/median runs by [F2], each using a height query and its inverse; step 2.1 supplies their logarithmic membership cost. Since $R/\delta$ is a fixed constant times a product of powers of $n$, $1/\rho$, $R/r$ and $R/\eta$, its logarithm is $O(\log((n/\rho)(R/\eta)(R/r)))$. Initial queries and the scalar branch are absorbed because the displayed logarithms are bounded below by positive constants. This proves the first bound, counting forward and inverse calls separately and then adding them.

The separator conversion [F1] therefore gives, on this event, a unit inward normal $s$ with $\langle s,z\rangle\ge\langle s,x\rangle-5\eta/6-2R\varepsilon/r$ on all of $K$. The input precision implies $2R\varepsilon/r<\eta/100$, so the additional encoded direction/rotation slack $\eta/100$ in [F4] still leaves error below $\eta$. Emit $G=-s$ in the original coordinates. This gives $\langle G,z\rangle\le\langle G,x\rangle+\eta$ on $K$, in particular on its inward $\eta$-erosion, with the OUT assertion already justified in step 1.1. Together with the IN branch this is exactly [F3]. The rational-direction encoding in [F4] specifies an exact unit normal by normalization; its output approximation was charged in the displayed slack.

For optimization, [F5] makes at most $BT$ adaptive weak-separation calls at precision $\eta_*$ and per-call failure $\rho_*$. Each is implemented by the first part with the stated $\varepsilon_*$; the conditional oracle guarantee is uniform over its input point and completed membership oracle, so the classical adaptive reduction applies. Its failure accounting and output guarantee are exactly those proved in [F5]. Now $BT=O(n\log(nR/s)(1+\log(R/\zeta)))$ and $s=r\zeta/(128R)$, while $1/\eta_*$ and $1/\rho_*$ have only polynomial dependence on these radius/precision ratios, $n$, and $1/\nu$. Multiplying by step 3.2 therefore gives the claimed $\widetilde O(n)$ membership queries. This multiplication charges every call; it imports neither the stronger arithmetic bound from a cited cutting-plane paper nor a free centroid operation.
