Let $B(x,t)=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\|z-x\|_2\le t\}$ and let $B(K,t)=\bigcup_{x\in K}B(x,t)$ for $t\ge0$; $B(K,-t)$ denotes the inward erosion consisting of points whose radius-$t$ ball is contained in $K$. A convex body is a closed convex set with nonempty interior. Assume rationally encoded $0<r\le R$ and $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$. The deterministic weak-membership oracle $\mathrm{MEM}_{\varepsilon,0}(K)$ is queried at a finite-precision point $y$ and must correctly assert either $y\in B(K,\varepsilon)$ or $y\notin B(K,-\varepsilon)$. In the overlap it may return either valid assertion. The coherent interface is a supplied reversible Boolean unitary with a fixed deterministic completion on every encoded input, together with its inverse and any controlled forms used.

A weak separation oracle $\mathrm{SEP}_{\eta,\rho}(K)$, queried at $y$, with probability at least $1-\rho$, either asserts $y\in B(K,\eta)$ or asserts $y\notin B(K,-\eta)$ and returns a unit vector $g$ satisfying $\langle g,z\rangle\le\langle g,y\rangle+\eta$ for every $z\in B(K,-\eta)$. The membership-to-separation algorithm is promised only on the query domain in its theorem; no unique answer is required in the boundary bands. A finite unit-normal encoding may be a nonzero rational vector v with the normalization g=v/||v|| interpreted exactly; rational bisection supplies an upper norm bound N between ||v|| and2||v|| when a classical reduction requires rational halfspaces. Radius, point, unit-normal and offset encodings and all query/inverse/gate/bit costs are part of the contract.

This specifies oracle behavior; a membership-to-separation theorem and any separation-to-optimization composition are separate claims with their own hypotheses.
Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Then there is a unique $p\in C$ such that $\|x-p\|_2\le\|x-z\|_2$ for every $z\in C$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

derivations.claim: Compactness of $K$ makes each nonempty vertical section compact, so its minimum exists; projection makes $C$ compact and convex. Convex combinations of two minimizing boundary points show convexity of $h$. For $\|y\|\le r$, the inner ball supplies a point at height zero, while the outer ball bounds all heights below by $-R$. Thus $-R\le h(y)\le0$ on that ball.

More generally on $B(0,d)$, $0<d<r$, let $y,y'$ be distinct and extend the directed line from $y$ through $y'$ by $r-d$ to $p=y'+(r-d)(y'-y)/\|y'-y\|$. Then $p\in B(0,r)$ and convexity on the segment $[y,p]$ gives $h(y')-h(y)\le R\|y'-y\|/(r-d)$. Exchange $y,y'$ and put $d=r/2$ to obtain the Lipschitz claim.

The ball $B((y,0),r/2)$ lies in $K$. Its convex hull with $(y,h(y))$ contains a ball of radius $\theta r/2$ about $(y,(1-\theta)h(y))$ for every $0\le\theta\le1$: combine the vertex with every point of that ball. Consequently all heights between $h(y)(1-2\varepsilon/r)$ and $-r/2$ lie in the inward $\varepsilon$-erosion, whenever this interval is nonempty. If $\varepsilon\ge r/2$ the claimed OUT bound is automatic from $h(y)\ge-R$ and $t\le-r/2$. For $0<\varepsilon<r/2$, write $H=-h(y)\le R$. If the interval is empty, then $H(1-2\varepsilon/r)<r/2$, so $H-r/2<2H\varepsilon/r\le2R\varepsilon/r$; every $t\le-r/2$ therefore satisfies $t<h(y)+2R\varepsilon/r$. If the interval is nonempty, OUT excludes its heights, so $t\le h(y)(1-2\varepsilon/r)\le h(y)+2R\varepsilon/r$. This uses an inclusion of balls, not an incorrect identity for the erosion of a cone.

For completeness, subgradients here need no arbitrary selection. The truncated epigraph $E=\{(y,t):y\in C,\ h(y)\le t\le R+1\}$ is compact and convex: it is the image of the compact set of pairs consisting of a point of $K$ and a permitted upward vertical displacement. Fix interior $y$ and $p=(y,h(y))$. Let $p_j=p-e_n/j$, and let $q_j$ be its unique nearest point in $E$ by [F2]. Minimality along a segment gives $\langle q_j-p_j,w-q_j\rangle\ge0$ for all $w\in E$, by expanding squared distance and taking the right derivative at zero. Moreover $\|q_j-p\|\le2/j$. A subsequence of the unit normals $(q_j-p_j)/\|q_j-p_j\|$ converges by [F3] to a unit normal $(u,t)$ with $\langle(u,t),w-p\rangle\ge0$ on $E$. Upward vertical segments imply $t\ge0$; if $t=0$, interior displacements of $y$ in both horizontal directions force $u=0$, a contradiction. Thus $t>0$ and $-u/t$ is a subgradient of $h$ on $C$. At a point where the Lipschitz bound holds on a neighborhood, applying the subgradient inequality in the directions $\pm p/\|p\|$ gives $\|p\|\le L$.

Fix $\|y\|\le r/2$. A subgradient $p$ of norm at most $2R/r$ gives the supporting inequality $\langle(-p,1),(z,t')-(y,h(y))\rangle\ge0$ on $K$. If $(y,t)$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $K$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $t\ge h(y)-\varepsilon\|(-p,1)\|\ge h(y)-3R\varepsilon/r$. This proves the IN implication, also at the transverse-ball boundary by the bound from step 2.1 on slightly larger balls and passage to its limit.

Maintain endpoints $\ell,u$. Initially $\ell=-R\le h(y)+2\delta/3$ and $u=-r/2\ge h(y)-\delta$. An IN answer replaces $u$ by the midpoint and preserves its lower bound by step 4.1; OUT replaces $\ell$ and preserves its upper bound by step 2.2. When $u-\ell\le\delta/3$, these invariants give $h(y)-\delta\le u\le h(y)+\delta$. Each iteration halves the bracket, proving the logarithmic query count. Fixed finite arithmetic and the deterministic oracle completion make the whole binary-search transcript a function of the input label. Store its transcript, copy its output, and reverse its computation and oracle calls; this implements that value oracle with clean work and only a constant factor more queries.

Write $z=(y,t)\in K$. Evaluating the approximate-subgradient premise at $y=0$ gives $b\ge0$. Since $a\ge0$ and $\|y\|\le R$, that inequality gives $\langle(-v,1),z\rangle=t-\langle v,y\rangle\ge h(0)-aR-b$. At $x=(0,-\|x\|)$ the OUT implication gives $h(0)\ge-\|x\|-2R\varepsilon/r$; if its height is below $-R$, this inequality follows directly from $h(0)\ge-R$. Divide by $\|(-v,1)\|\ge1$ to obtain the stated separation inequality.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be mutually independent Bernoulli$(p_i)$ variables on a finite probability space. Set $S=\sum_iX_i$ and $\mu=\sum_i p_i$. For $\delta\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(S\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le\exp\{-\mu((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta)\}.$$
For $0\le\delta<1$,
$$\mathbb P(S\le(1-\delta)\mu)\le\exp\{-\mu(\delta+(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta))\}.$$
For $0\le\delta\le1$ the upper and lower tails are respectively at most $\exp(-\mu\delta^2/3)$ and $\exp(-\mu\delta^2/2)$, and
$$\mathbb P(|S-\mu|\ge\delta\mu)\le2\exp(-\mu\delta^2/3).$$
At $\delta=1$ the lower optimized bound is $\exp(-\mu)$, proved directly rather than by taking $\log0$. Empty sums and $\mu=0$ are included. Also, for $N>0$ and $t\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(|S-\mu|\ge t)\le2\exp(-2t^2/N).$$

$$2^{-n/2}\sum_{y=0}^{2^n-1}e^{2\pi ixy/2^n}|y\rangle,$$

with the declared output register order. Hence its denotation is $\operatorname{QFT}_{2^n}$ on every state. Reversing the gate list and replacing every gate by its adjoint gives the negative-sign inverse QFT with the same ideal gate count.

For an integer $N\ge1$, let $\mathcal F_N$ be the negative-sign, $N^{-1/2}$-normalized transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]. Define the **cyclic quantum Fourier transform** by $\operatorname{QFT}_N:=\mathcal F_N^{-1}$. The inverse exists by [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]], and its matrix on the standard basis indexed by $0,\ldots,N-1$ is

$$\operatorname{QFT}_N|x\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{y=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ixy/N}|y\rangle,\qquad 0\le x<N.$$

Here the standard-basis ket convention is the one specified by [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. Thus the transform has the positive sign and the same $N^{-1/2}$ normalization as the inverse Fourier formula. At $N=1$ it is the identity on the one-dimensional register. In the binary specialization $N=2^n$, the circuit page writes each index in its unique base-two expansion.
The circle constant satisfies $3<\pi<22/7$.

derivations.claim: Put $\tau=r_2$, $D_i(z)=(f(z+\tau e_i)-2f(z)+f(z-\tau e_i))/\tau^2$, $D=\sum_iD_i$, and $p_i(z)=(f(z+\tau e_i)-f(z-\tau e_i))/(2\tau)$. The bound on $\delta$ gives $\tau\le r_1$. Convexity makes every $D_i\ge0$. On the query rectangle each $D_i$ and $D$ is a finite linear combination of translates of the $L$-Lipschitz function $f$, hence is Lipschitz there; all sections are likewise Lipschitz and Riemann integrable. Uniform grid Darboux sums have gaps bounded by the Lipschitz constant times cell diameter times total volume, so [F1] applies. For $d=1$, use the one-dimensional integral directly; for $d\ge2$, apply [F1] to the first coordinate and the remaining $d-1$ coordinates. On any coordinate line, cancellation of shifted integrals leaves two pairs of boundary strips of length $\tau$. The absolute value of each pair is at most $L\tau^2$, so $\int_{-r_1}^{r_1}(f(t+\tau)-2f(t)+f(t-\tau))dt\le2L\tau^2$. Thus $\mathbb E D(Z)\le dL/r_1\le nL/r_1$ for uniform $Z$.

Coupling $Z$ to its cell center $z$, each of the four terms in a second difference moves by at most its Lipschitz constant times $\sqrt d\,h_0/2$. Thus $|D(z)-D(Z)|\le4n^2Lh_0/\tau^2\le(\rho/1000)L/(2r_1)$. For the finite uniform center distribution, Markov's inequality follows by summing its nonnegative weights. Therefore $D(z)\le2nL/(\rho_0r_1)$ except with probability at most $\rho_0/2+(\rho/1000)\rho_0/(4n)$.

Fix such a good center. On the symmetric points $\pm\tau e_i$, the convex function $q(u)=f(z+u)-f(z)-\langle p(z),u\rangle$ has value $\tau^2D_i(z)/2\le\tau^2D(z)/2$. Every point of the $\ell_1$ ball of radius $\tau$ is a convex combination of these points. Convexity gives the upper bound there; applying convexity to $u,-u$ and $q(0)=0$ gives the same lower bound. Hence $|q(u)|\le\tau^2D(z)/2\le\delta$ on that ball. The cube $a[-1/2,1/2]^d$ lies in it. Lipschitzness gives $|p_i(z)|\le L$.

Put $\gamma=ap(z)/(3B_*)$; then $\|\gamma\|_\infty\le1/3$. The ideal affine phase on the product grid produces independent one-coordinate Fourier distributions centered at $M\gamma_i$. For an integer output at circular distance $D$ from this center, summing the geometric progression gives probability $\sin^2(\pi M\gamma_i)/(M^2\sin^2(\pi D/M))\le1/(4D^2)$ for $0<D\le M/2$. Thus the probability of circular error greater than four is at most $\frac12\sum_{j\ge4}j^{-2}\le1/6$, since $j^{-2}\le1/(j(j-1))$ for $j\ge4$ and $\sum_{j\ge4}1/(j(j-1))=1/3$ by telescoping. Because $M\ge32$ and $|\gamma_i|\le1/3$, the signed interval endpoints are farther than four from the center; circular error at most four therefore also gives ordinary signed error at most four.

The affine error from step 3.1 plus value error is at most $2\delta$. Since $B_*=28\pi\delta M$, the phase angle perturbation is at most $1/21$ at every address. The Euclidean distance of the resulting unit vectors is at most $1/21$; a measurement event changes by at most that distance, as follows by resolving the two pure states in their two-dimensional span and maximizing the projection difference. The allowed implemented-phase operator error adds at most $1/1000$. Each coordinate therefore has ordinary signed error at most four with probability greater than $1-1/6-1/21-1/1000>2/3$. The decoded gradient error on this event is at most $12B_* /(aM)=336\pi\delta/a$.

For fixed $z$, the runs are independent trials for this same coordinate, not independently sampled target functions. A median fails only if at least half the runs fail. The bound from [F2] is at most $2e^{-N/18}$, because the expected bad count is at most $N/3$ and the excess is at least $N/6$. The chosen count and a union bound give simultaneous coordinate accuracy except with probability at most $\rho/500$. Every phase run uses one value query and its inverse, giving $2N\le36\ln(1000n/\rho)+8=O(\log(n/\rho))$ calls combined.

Let $s$ be any subgradient at the good center. Applying [F5] at the two coordinate offsets yields $|s_i-p_i(z)|\le\tau D_i(z)/2$, hence $\|s-p(z)\|_\infty\le nL\tau/(\rho_0r_1)$. Add the gradient error from step 6.1 and use $\tau^2=\delta r_1\rho_0/(nL)$. This gives $\|s-v\|_\infty\le(1+168\pi)\sqrt{\delta n^3L/(\rho_0r_1)}<23^2\sqrt{\delta n^3L/(\rho_0r_1)}$ by [F4].

The subgradient inequality gives $f(y)\ge f(z)+\langle s,y-z\rangle$. Both $|f(z)-f(0)|$ and $|\langle s,z\rangle|$ are at most $L\sqrt n r_1$. Replacing $s$ by $v$ costs at most $\|s-v\|_\infty\|y\|_1\le\sqrt n\|s-v\|_\infty\|y\|$. Step 7.1 gives exactly the displayed inequality. The total failure is at most $\rho_0/2+(\rho/1000)\rho_0/(4n)+\rho/500<\rho$. The query count is that of step 6.1; choosing the finite shift costs no function query.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be
nonempty compact convex sets. With $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ and
$\lambda_d$ denoting Lebesgue measure,
$$\lambda_d(A+B)^{1/d}\ge \lambda_d(A)^{1/d}+\lambda_d(B)^{1/d}.$$
Zero-volume and lower-dimensional sets are included.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $B(x,t)=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\|z-x\|_2\le t\}$ and let $B(K,t)=\bigcup_{x\in K}B(x,t)$ for $t\ge0$; $B(K,-t)$ denotes the inward erosion consisting of points whose radius-$t$ ball is contained in $K$. A convex body is a closed convex set with nonempty interior. Assume rationally encoded $0<r\le R$ and $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$. The deterministic weak-membership oracle $\mathrm{MEM}_{\varepsilon,0}(K)$ is queried at a finite-precision point $y$ and must correctly assert either $y\in B(K,\varepsilon)$ or $y\notin B(K,-\varepsilon)$. In the overlap it may return either valid assertion. The coherent interface is a supplied reversible Boolean unitary with a fixed deterministic completion on every encoded input, together with its inverse and any controlled forms used.

A weak separation oracle $\mathrm{SEP}_{\eta,\rho}(K)$, queried at $y$, with probability at least $1-\rho$, either asserts $y\in B(K,\eta)$ or asserts $y\notin B(K,-\eta)$ and returns a unit vector $g$ satisfying $\langle g,z\rangle\le\langle g,y\rangle+\eta$ for every $z\in B(K,-\eta)$. The membership-to-separation algorithm is promised only on the query domain in its theorem; no unique answer is required in the boundary bands. A finite unit-normal encoding may be a nonzero rational vector v with the normalization g=v/||v|| interpreted exactly; rational bisection supplies an upper norm bound N between ||v|| and2||v|| when a classical reduction requires rational halfspaces. Radius, point, unit-normal and offset encodings and all query/inverse/gate/bit costs are part of the contract.

This specifies oracle behavior; a membership-to-separation theorem and any separation-to-optimization composition are separate claims with their own hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Let $P$ be a full-dimensional compact convex body and $X$ uniform on $P$. For any unit $a$, the survival function $S(t)=\Pr(\langle a,X\rangle\ge t)$ is log-concave on the open projection interval: the Minkowski interpolation of the two caps at $t_0,t_1$ lies in the cap at their interpolated threshold, so [F1] gives concavity of $S^{1/n}$, and the increasing concave logarithm gives concavity of $\log S$. Slices and [F3] show that the projected distribution has continuous strictly increasing cumulative distribution on that interval and no atoms. Consequently $S(\langle a,X\rangle)$ is uniform on $(0,1)$, by inverting this strictly monotone continuous function. Thus $\mathbb E[-\log S(\langle a,X\rangle)]=\int_0^1-\log t\,dt=1$. Jensen [F2] yields $S(\langle a,\mathbb EX\rangle)\ge e^{-1}$. Applying this to $-a$ shows that either halfspace through the centroid contains at least $1/e$ of the volume.

If $P$ contains a radius-$s$ ball, its width in every direction is at least $2s$. The projected density is at most $n/(2s)$. Indeed, for $n\ge2$ the $(n-1)$-slice area to the power $1/(n-1)$ is concave by [F1]. A slice of area $A$ at position $t$ therefore gives cone lower bounds $A((v-a)/(t-a))^{n-1}$ to its left and $A((b-v)/(b-t))^{n-1}$ to its right, where $[a,b]$ is the projection interval. Integrating gives $\operatorname{vol}(P)\ge A(b-a)/n$. Taking limits at endpoints proves the density bound for every interior slice. For $n=1$ the density is $1/(b-a)$ directly. A slab of thickness $h$ thus has relative volume at most $nh/(2s)$.

Choose a rational vector $v$ with $\|v-c\|\le\zeta/(64R)$, so $\|v\|\le2$. For a rational threshold $\gamma$, initialize a localization polytope $P=[-R,R]^n$ and make at most $T$ iterations. If it is empty or lower-dimensional, return FAIL. Otherwise compute its exact centroid $p_0$ and round to a fixed-point rational $p$ with $\|p-p_0\|\le\eta$. If $\langle v,p\rangle<\gamma$, keep $P\cap\{x:\langle v,x\rangle\ge\langle v,p\rangle\}$ without an oracle call. Otherwise query weak separation at $p$: IN returns $p$ as a witness; on an OUT answer in rational direction $u$, keep $P\cap\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\le\langle u,p\rangle+\eta N\}$. After $T$ iterations without a witness, return FAIL. All constraints are rational. Every retained polytope contains $F_\gamma=B(K,-\eta)\cap\{x:\langle v,x\rangle\ge\gamma\}$ whenever the oracle answers succeed. The oracle cut has geometric displacement at most $3\eta$ from the true centroid, including point rounding; the objective cut has displacement at most $\eta$. Common fixed-point query registers can therefore be chosen from the bounded initial box and this explicit rounding precision, despite growth of the internal exact centroid denominators.

This is a finite arithmetic procedure. Vertices of a bounded rational polytope are found by enumerating all subsets of $n$ defining hyperplanes, solving each nonsingular linear system, and retaining feasible solutions. A nonempty full-dimensional bounded polytope has vertices, since successively minimizing coordinates on a minimizing face eventually gives a zero-dimensional face. Supporting facets can be enumerated from its finite vertex list and checked by rational sign tests. Triangulate a facet inductively by choosing one vertex and coning its nonincident boundary facets; then cone the resulting boundary simplices to a rational interior point such as the average of all vertices. This partitions $P$ up to common faces. A simplex has volume $|\det(v_1-v_0,\ldots,v_n-v_0)|/n!$ and centroid $(v_0+\cdots+v_n)/(n+1)$: the first identity is [F3], and the second follows by permutation symmetry of barycentric coordinates and their sum being one. The volume-weighted average of these simplex centroids is the exact rational centroid of $P$. Dimensions, incidences, and zero determinants are decided by finite rational elimination. No efficiency of this enumeration is asserted.

Put $h=\max_{x\in K}\langle v,x\rangle$ and take a maximizer $x_*$. If $\gamma\le h-\tau$, let $\alpha=\tau/(8R)$ and $z=(1-\alpha)x_*$. Convexity gives $B(z,\alpha r)\subset K$. Since $s=\alpha r/2$ and $\eta\le s$, the ball $B(z,s)$ lies in $B(K,-\eta)$. Also $\langle v,z\rangle\ge h-\alpha|h|\ge h-\tau/4$, and its value on that ball drops by at most $2s\le\tau/8$. Therefore $F_\gamma$ contains this radius-$s$ ball.

Under this condition, every localization polytope contains the ball from step 2.2. The rounded-centroid objective and oracle cuts remove at least $1/e-n(3\eta)/(2s)=1/e-3/200>1/4$ of the volume by step 1.1 and step 1.2. Thus each nonterminating iteration leaves at most $3/4$ of the volume. But the radius-$s$ ball contains a cube of side $2s/n$, whereas after $T$ cuts the volume is less than $(2s/n)^n$ by the defining rational test for $T$. This is impossible. Hence FAIL implies $\gamma>h-\tau$ on successful oracle answers; IN returns a witness in $B(K,\eta)$ with $\langle v,p\rangle\ge\gamma$.
